passage:
In the courtyard of their Aliganj building, Ujjwal bhaiya set up a chessboard on an upturned bucket and showed Parveen how the knight jumps. By Tuesday she knew every piece. By Thursday she had checkmated Ammi, who laughed and said she'd let her win. By Saturday she beat Ujjwal bhaiya's little cousin in twelve moves.
"I'm getting better every single day!" Parveen shouted, running up two flights of stairs to tell Abbu.
She drew a chessboard on the back of her maths notebook and practised knight jumps during recess. That night, under the blanket, she whispered, "Next week I'll beat Ujjwal bhaiya. Then the state championship."

qa.q: Where did Ujjwal bhaiya set up the chessboard?
qa.a: On an upturned bucket in the courtyard of their Aliganj building.

qa.q: How does Parveen feel after her first week of chess, and how can you tell?
qa.a: She feels thrilled and proud 😊; she shouts that she is getting better every day and runs upstairs to tell Abbu.

qa.q: How could Ujjwal bhaiya keep Parveen's excitement healthy as her expectations rise?
qa.a: He could celebrate her fast progress but gently mention that learning slows later and that losing games is part of getting better.

qa.q: What might Ujjwal bhaiya think when he hears Parveen plans to beat him next week?
qa.a: He might smile at her confidence and feel pleased his lessons sparked such excitement, while knowing harder games lie ahead.

grounding: Shows a child's quick early wins at chess, where every step feels like a victory and her expectations quietly climb.

passage:
"Seema didi, look! I made the cat walk across the screen!"
Seema leaned over the old laptop. "Wait, you did that yourself?"
"Yes! It's block coding. Ten minutes and I made him walk. Now watch, I'm making him say hello."
"Leela, dinner!" Papa called.
"Two minutes, Papa! I just have to make him jump!"
"Since when do you skip dinner for homework?"
"It's not homework, it's coding! Yesterday I didn't even know what a loop was, and today I made a loop!"
Seema laughed. "Okay, genius."
"Tomorrow I'll make a whole game. With levels. And a score." Leela's eyes were shining. "By Diwali I'll make a game like the ones on your phone."
"By Diwali?" Papa said, coming to the door. "That's three weeks."
"Easy," Leela said, dragging another block into place.

qa.q: What did Leela make the cat do first?
qa.a: Leela made the cat walk across the screen.

qa.q: What does Leela's plan to make a game by Diwali suggest?
qa.a: Quick early wins have made Leela excited and very confident, so expectations are quietly rising beyond what three weeks may allow.

qa.q: How could Papa or Seema didi support Leela's excitement wisely?
qa.a: They could cheer each small win and help Leela pick a next step, like one level, so slower progress later doesn't feel like failure.

qa.q: How might Papa feel hearing 'Easy' about a game by Diwali?
qa.a: Papa may be amused and pleased at the enthusiasm, while quietly wondering how Leela will feel when it takes longer than three weeks.

grounding: Illustrates a child's fast early wins in block coding, easy motivation and rising expectations in a lively family scene.

passage:
At the community centre chess club, Shreya won her first game in week two. By week four she'd beaten three older kids.
"I can see the whole board now!" she told Nirmala ma'am, the coach.
"You're learning fast," Nirmala ma'am said.
Shreya practised every evening. Every new opening felt like a secret. Every game taught her a trick. She told her mother she'd be a champion by Diwali.
Nirmala ma'am smiled, but said gently, "Enjoy this part. Later it gets slower. That's normal too."
Shreya didn't really hear her. She was already setting up the pieces again.

qa.q: By which week had Shreya beaten three older kids?
qa.a: By week four.

qa.q: What was Shreya feeling as she set up the pieces again?
qa.a: Shreya felt excited and confident, thrilled by quick wins and dreaming big.

qa.q: What could help Shreya later, when progress slows?
qa.a: Remembering Nirmala ma'am's words that slower progress is normal, so she doesn't lose heart.

qa.q: What might Nirmala ma'am be thinking when she warns Shreya gently?
qa.a: Nirmala ma'am seems pleased but wise, knowing the early excitement won't last forever.

grounding: Shows a child beginning chess with quick early wins, easy motivation and quietly rising expectations.

passage:
Week one: Yusuf started a free coding class at school. By Friday he'd made a cat move across the screen. He ran home shouting, "Leela Apa, I made a game!"
Week two: He added a score and a jumping sound. Every evening he showed his sister something new. "Look, look!" She clapped every time.
Week three: Yusuf said he'd make a game as good as the ones on his cousin's phone by the summer holidays. Leela Apa raised an eyebrow. "By summer?" "Easy," said Yusuf, already clicking.

qa.q: What did Yusuf make move across the screen?
qa.a: A cat.

qa.q: What was Yusuf feeling in week three when he said "Easy"?
qa.a: He felt excited and confident, his expectations rising after quick early wins.

qa.q: What could help Yusuf when the learning gets harder?
qa.a: Knowing that early progress is fast and later progress slows, so he keeps going even when it's not easy.

qa.q: How might Leela Apa feel when he says "By summer"?
qa.a: Leela Apa is probably amused and a little doubtful, proud of him but aware it may be harder.

grounding: Shows a child starting coding with fast early gains, easy motivation and rising expectations over three weeks.

passage:
Manoj, beta, you've started tabla? Wonderful! Let me tell you about when I, your Reena Nani, started, when I was nine.
The first week, I learned "dha" and "na". The second week, a whole small pattern. My guruji said, "Very good, Reena!" I felt like a star. I practised every evening without anyone asking.
By the fourth week I told everyone I'd play at the temple festival. My mother laughed and said, "Let's see."
Beta, those first weeks are magic. Everything is new, every sound is a win. Enjoy it. But remember, later it gets slow, and that's when the real learning happens. I didn't play at that festival. I played at the next one.

qa.q: What were the first two sounds Reena learned?
qa.a: "Dha" and "na".

qa.q: What was young Reena feeling in the first weeks?
qa.a: Young Reena felt excited and proud, like a star, with every sound a win.

qa.q: In the story, what happened to Reena's big expectation?
qa.a: Young Reena had planned to play at the temple festival, but it took longer, and the first performance came at the next one instead.

qa.q: What might Reena's mother have been thinking when she said "Let's see"?
qa.a: Her mother was probably amused and gently doubtful, expecting the pace to slow.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling starting tabla as a child with quick early gains, easy motivation and rising expectations.

passage: The chess set at Harsha's house was missing a knight and two pawns, so Anand used a button and two coins instead. He didn't mind. In his first week he learned how every piece moved. By the second week he could spot a fork, and on Friday he beat Harsha's older brother for the first time, with a button knight. He ran all the way home shouting about it. That night he lay awake planning: district tournament by summer, state by next year. Maybe he would even be on television. Every day brought something new, and each new trick felt like a trophy. He didn't notice how fast his dreams had grown compared with the three short weeks he had been playing.

qa.q: What did Anand use in place of the missing knight?
qa.a: A button.

qa.q: How did Anand feel after beating Harsha's older brother?
qa.a: He was thrilled and proud, running all the way home shouting about it.

qa.q: What could help Anand keep enjoying chess once the quick wins slow down?
qa.a: Setting small goals, like learning one new idea a week instead of aiming at a state title, and expecting slower days later.

qa.q: How might Harsha's older brother feel about losing to a three-week beginner?
qa.a: He might be surprised or a little embarrassed, and perhaps impressed by Anand's quick progress.

grounding: Shows a child starting chess with quick early wins, easy motivation and expectations quietly racing ahead of three weeks of play.
